Estradiol and norethindrone acetate (oral) is a combination of estrogen and progestin that has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms due to menopause, moderate to severe symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy due to menopause, and for the prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis. 2. Common adverse reactions associated with this medication include edema, chloasma, hirsutism, loss of scalp hair, weight gain, abdominal pain, bloating, headache, breast tenderness, menstrual disorders, breast pain, breast swelling, vaginal discomfort, withdrawal bleeding, upper respiratory infections, and general pain. 3. When prescribing solely for the treatment of moderate to severe symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy due to menopause, topical vaginal products should be considered. 4. For the prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis, therapy should only be considered for women at significant risk of osteoporosis, and non-estrogen medications should be carefully evaluated. 5. The use of estrogen, alone or in combination with a progestin, should be at the lowest effective dose and for the shortest duration consistent with treatment goals and individual risk factors. Postmenopausal women should be periodically re-evaluated to determine if continued treatment is necessary. 6. Activella therapy consists of a single tablet taken once daily for the treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms due to menopause, moderate to severe symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy due to menopause, and for the prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis. 7. Activella is contraindicated in women with undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, known or suspected breast cancer, estrogen-dependent neoplasia, active or history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE), active or history of arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction), known hypersensitivity to the drug, liver impairment or disease, protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency, or known or suspected pregnancy. 8. Cardiovascular risks include an increased risk of DVT, PE, stroke, and myocardial infarction (MI) with estrogen plus progestin therapy. Estrogen-alone therapy has also been associated with an increased risk of stroke and DVT. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if any of these conditions occur or are suspected. 9. In the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) estrogen plus progestin sub-study, a statistically significant increased risk of stroke was observed in women aged 50 to 79 years receiving daily conjugated estrogens (CE) plus medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) compared to placebo. The increased risk persisted after the first year of use. 10. In the WHI estrogen-alone sub-study, a statistically significant increased risk of stroke was also observed in women aged 50 to 79 years receiving daily CE alone compared to placebo. Subgroup analyses suggested no increased risk of stroke in women aged 50 to 59 years receiving CE alone. 11. In the WHI estrogen plus progestin sub-study, there was a statistically non-significant increased risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) events in women receiving daily CE plus MPA compared to placebo. The relative risk was higher in the first year and decreased in subsequent years. 12. In the WHI estrogen-alone sub-study, no overall effect on CHD events was observed in women receiving CE alone compared to placebo. Subgroup analyses suggested a non-significant reduction in CHD events in women less than 10 years post-menopause. 13. In the WHI estrogen plus progestin sub-study, a statistically significant two-fold increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), including DVT and PE, was observed in women receiving daily CE plus MPA compared to placebo. The increased risk was evident during the first year and persisted. 14. In the WHI estrogen-alone sub-study, the risk of VTE was increased in women receiving CE alone compared to placebo, with a statistically significant increase in DVT risk. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if VTE occurs or is suspected. 15. Estrogen therapy may lead to severe hypercalcemia in patients with breast cancer and bone metastases. 16. Retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogens. Therapy should be discontinued if sudden partial or complete loss of vision, proptosis, diplopia, or migraine occurs. If examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions, estrogens should be permanently discontinued. 17. The addition of a progestin to estrogen therapy in postmenopausal women with a uterus has been shown to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia, a potential precursor to endometrial cancer. However, the use of progestins may increase the risk of breast cancer. 18. Estrogen therapy may exacerbate conditions such as asthma, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, migraine, porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas. Caution is advised in women with these conditions. 19. Estrogen therapy may cause fluid retention, which could exacerbate conditions such as cardiac or renal impairment. Careful observation is warranted in such cases. 20. Women with pre-existing hypertriglyceridemia may experience elevated plasma triglycerides leading to pancreatitis during estrogen therapy. Discontinuation of therapy should be considered if pancreatitis occurs. 21. Estrogen therapy may lead to increased thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels, requiring adjustments in thyroid hormone replacement therapy for women dependent on it. Thyroid function should be monitored to maintain free thyroid hormone levels within the normal range. 22. Estrogen therapy has been associated with an increased risk of abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation. Women should undergo regular breast examinations and mammography based on age, risk factors, and prior results. 23. In the WHI estrogen plus progestin sub-study, an increased risk of invasive breast cancer was observed in women receiving daily CE plus MPA compared to placebo. The risk was higher among women with prior hormone therapy use. 24. In the WHI estrogen-alone sub-study, no increased risk of invasive breast cancer was observed in women receiving CE alone compared to placebo after an average follow-up of 7.1 years. 25. Observational studies suggest an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy and a smaller increased risk with estrogen-alone therapy after several years of use. The risk appears to return to baseline approximately five years after stopping therapy. 26. A statistically non-significant increased risk of ovarian cancer was reported in the WHI estrogen plus progestin sub-study. Observational studies have also associated prolonged use of estrogen plus progestin or estrogen-alone products with an increased risk of ovarian cancer. 27. In the WHI Memory Study (WHIMS), an increased risk of probable dementia was observed in women aged 65 to 79 years receiving CE plus MPA or CE alone compared to placebo. It is unknown whether these findings apply to younger postmenopausal women. 28. A 2to 4-fold increased risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery has been reported in postmenopausal women receiving estrogens. 29. Estradiol and norethindrone acetate (oral) therapy may cause adverse reactions such as changes in vaginal bleeding patterns, breast tenderness, nausea, headache, and mood disturbances.
